title: AIMS: An uncertainty-aware AI experimentalist for quantum matter
authors: Siyuan Qiu, Philip D. Suh, Nhat Huy Tran, Xirui Wang, Heonjoon Park, Kutay Akin, Kevin K. S. Multani, Seungwon Jung, Wenkai Cai, Xinyu Liu, Ziyan Zhu, Chunjing Jia, Zhantao Chen, Zhixun Shen, Zhurun Ji
abstract: Autonomous scientific agents are beginning to accelerate discovery, but most demonstrations operate in digital or highly structured settings where the objects, actions, and objectives are largely predefined. Quantum materials experiments pose a harder problem where uncertainties involve: the instrument state can drift, the useful signal may occupy only rare regions of an inhomogeneous sample, and the physical mechanism is often under-determined. Here we introduce the AI agent for Inference and Measurement in Science (AIMS), an uncertainty-aware closed-loop AI experimentalist for cryogenic microwave impedance microscopy that converts uncertainty into experimental action. AIMS links three nested loops: navigation under uncertain perception, measurement selection under sample inhomogeneity, and scale-resolved mechanism attribution under ambiguous physics. In navigation, it relocates the sample after cryogenic displacement, flags unreliable position estimates, and invokes recovery strategies, significantly reducing sample-locating time. In measurement, it maps twist angle distribution and generalized Wigner crystal score of twisted bilayer MoSe$_2$ to identify regions with the strongest correlated response. In discovery, AIMS asks not whether melting is simply classical or quantum, but how the competition of Coulomb repulsion, hopping, and other energy scales shapes the observed hierarchy. By testing the classical limit, varying hopping and Coulomb scales, and preserving sample morphology as a secondary testable variable, AIMS prioritizes a quantum-fluctuation-renormalized origin of the anomalously robust $ν= 1/2$ crystal. AIMS demonstrates uncertainty-aware experimental agency for quantum matter with perception recovery, measurement choice, and energy-scale-resolved mechanism attribution in one closed loop.
summary: This work introduces AIMS, an advanced AI agent that autonomously guides experiments on quantum materials to resolve fundamental physical questions. By integrating perception recovery, targeted measurement selection based on local disorder, and iterative hypothesis testing, it successfully identified the role of quantum fluctuations in stabilizing fractional Wigner crystal states.
main_problem: To autonomously discover the physical mechanism responsible for the anomalous stability of fractional Wigner crystal states in quantum materials.
main_result:
The study demonstrates that the exceptional robustness of the $
u=1/2$ state is primarily due to quantum-fluctuation renormalization effects involving electron hopping, rather than purely classical charge ordering.
method: An uncertainty-aware closed-loop AI agent (AIMS) was developed to guide experiments by managing perception errors, selecting optimal measurement sites based on local inhomogeneity, and iteratively refining physical hypotheses.
model_or_system: The system involves twisted bilayer $	ext{MoSe}_2$ moiré superlattices exhibiting correlated insulating states. The analysis compares results from classical Monte Carlo simulations against advanced quantum models like Hartree-Fock and Exact Diagonalization.
key_observables:
Melting temperature ($T_m$) hierarchy across different filling factors ($
u=1/3, 1/2, 2/3$), Generalized Wigner Crystal (GWC) score maps, and local twist angle distributions.
important_parameters: Twist angle disorder ($	heta \approx 3.13^\circ$), hopping energy ($t$), Coulomb repulsion strength, and various energy scale ratios used in theoretical models.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that the physical mechanism can be uncovered by iteratively testing hypotheses and quantifying uncertainty across multiple experimental passes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate AIMS's three nested loops (Navigation, Measurement Selection via GWC scoring, Discovery/Hypothesis Testing), showing recovery from poor data quality using GP reconstruction and comparing model predictions against measured $T_m$ values.
paper_structure: The paper is structured around the AIMS framework: first demonstrating robust navigation under uncertainty; second, narrowing down measurement regions on inhomogeneous samples (GWC scoring); and finally, executing a closed-loop discovery process to distinguish between competing physical mechanisms governing correlated states.
why_interesting: It provides a blueprint for how AI can tackle complex many-body physics problems by systematically mapping out the parameter space of uncertainty, which is crucial for understanding emergent quantum phases in strongly correlated systems.
